utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Hannis, is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We are, Your Honour. I understood from Mr. Stewart there was one matter he wanted to raise with you before we began.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'll give an opportunity for Mr. Stewart to raise the matter he has in mind

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm just for the moment trying to find a microphone that works easily. It was only this, Your Honour, just for a couple of minutes. It was just to say -- Your Honours may know that we put in some fairly short submissions yesterday on the self-representation issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have not seen them yet. But I take it that I'll see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I hope, so Your Honour, through the normal channels. It was filed yesterday afternoon and it annexes the notes on the United States and English cases, but it's also -- it's -- Your Honour, in effect -- I've explained to the Prosecution this: It's a summary of where we say we've got to now, basically..

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But Your Honours will see. There's no point in my elaborating because it will find its way to Your Honours. And the only thing I wanted to mention is that Ms. Loukas is going to deal with this witness this morning. But in relation to all these issues of self-representation and particularly the sort of matters that have been raised by Mr. Krajisnik in his letters to the Trial Chamber, Your Honour, this is -- this is not an area in which both of us, Ms. Loukas and I, have been heavily involved. I keep Ms. Loukas informed, but Your Honours will appreciate that many of those matters are distinctly lead counsel' responsibility, and in the interest of not wasting resources, we don't both deal with that. So, Your Honour, if anything does come up in this area, I'm very rarely more than 20 minutes away, if the Court should need to deal with the matter at any time. And, of course, I'm at the -- the Trial Chamber's disposal. But I would particularly ask in that area that if -- if matters such as that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- do arise, that I could be alerted and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I do understand that you -- that you are -- standby. This is not the same as being standby counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. All right, thank you very much for that, Your Honour. I shall -- if I may, I shall leave at some point, I hope discreetly, quite soon, though I am going to stay for a short while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Hannis, are you ready to call your next witness? Is there anything -- would there be anything that should be dealt with in the absence of the witness prior to calling him in? Ms. Loukas, I'm not soliciting, but ...

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's no need to solicit because there is an issue a and significant issue that needs to be dealt with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: -- in the absence of the witness and prior to the commencement of the witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I can indicate, Your Honour, this was a witness that was initially scheduled for viva voce evidence. The Prosecution now wishes to proceed by way of 89(F) in part. And in those circumstances, Your Honour, I can indicate that the Defence vigorously opposes any attempt to use 89(F) in respect of this witness. Your Honour, it's -- it's a situation whereby, as Your Honours are well aware, it was -- and I can go further into what my arguments, if Your Honour wishes at this stage, or if Your Honour wishes to hear Mr. Hannis's response prior to my going into the matters that I wish to go into.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps you briefly could explain why you consider 89(F) not suitable for this witness, and then please concentrate on the question why partial 89(F) would be unacceptable and why the whole of the testimony should be led without the use of 89(F).

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll keep Your Honour's injunction in mind. Now, firstly, of course, Your Honour, this is an area that was dealt with on appeal from the Milosevic Trial Chamber, and it is, of course, the -- the issue in the context of -- that Justice Judge Hunt gave his famous dissenting opinion about the nature of the decision by the full Appeals Chamber and the spreading stain that it would leave on the reputation of this Tribunal. Going from there to what the Appeals Chamber actually held, Your Honour -- and I'd point Your Honours to this matter, and that is that it was indicated in terms of whilst the discretion on the part of the Trial Chamber is available, Your Honour, the Appeals Chamber decision itself did not in fact circumscribe in any detail the matters that do go to the specific exercise of the discretion. Now, Your Honour, what they did indicate was that it was -- should be exercised in the interests of justice and also that -- in the interests of justice and two matters that were specifically enumerated in the majority Appeals Chamber decision was acts and conduct of the accused and the surrounding circumstances. Now, firstly in relation to acts and conduct of the accused, Your Honour, this is not a statement that contains some passing reference to Mr. Krajisnik. This is a statement, Your Honour, that is flooded with references to Mr. Krajisnik, firstly. Secondly, in the context of a witness of this nature and the numerous references to Mr. Krajisnik, to assert in any meaningful way that in some way it's divisible in these circumstances is, in my submission, Your Honour, not a position that can be taken on any reasonable basis. When one counts -- even if one were to go to superficial numerical exercise of counting the numbers of reference to Mr. Krajisnik throughout this statement, we are dealing with a statement that in no real sense is divisible. The matters are inextricably intertwined and should be the subject of proper viva voce evidence led by the Prosecution without leading questions, and, Your Honour, it's simply not the sort of evidence that can be allowed to proceed in this shorthand fashion. Secondly, surrounding circumstances, Your Honour. If one looks at the surrounding circumstances of this particular witness, this particular witness, Your Honour, was requested by the Prosecution in April of this year. This is not a witness that has been on the timetable for quite some time now. This is a witness that is only recent. This was a request for a new viva voce witness by the Prosecution in the middle of April of this year. Now, Your Honour, that's -- that's a very specific and important matter that goes to the surrounding circumstances because this is also a matter that requires, and quite clearly requires, investigation by the Defence, and proper investigation, and it's not the sort of evidence that can be dealt with in this perfunctory truncated fashion under 89(F). And as I've indicated previously, to -- to assert that it is divisible is, in my most respectful opinion -- cannot be asserted on any reasonable basis. So, Your Honour, there we have it. In my submission, taking into account what was specifically stated in the majority decision in the Appeals Chamber decision, look at interests of justice, look at the surrounding circumstances, look at acts and conduct of the accused. I've addressed Your Honours on those matters. In addition, Your Honour, it's -- it's quite clear that even though Your Honours have a discretion in this circumstance, that certainly does not mean that this is the sort of evidence that should just be brought forward in this way. It is not divisible. It is not appropriate. And it is not in the interests of justice, Your Honours. And I would also indicate that if for some reason the Prosecution would think that this is some sort of time-saving exercise, I can indicate that it would not be, Your Honours. Your Honours are well aware that I have just completed the cross-examination of a significant expert. That was a witness that Mr. Tieger dealt with for the Prosecution. The Prosecution go on to have another attorney for the next witness. I have to deal with both. That's because we're a limited Defence team. I will in any event require this weekend so that I can be in a position to cross-examine this witness, and that is a matter very much in the interests of justice, when one takes into account the limited resources of the Defence in comparison with the Prosecution. So I'll also make that point about potential time-savings. Your Honour, in my submission, they do not exist. So, Your Honours, in conclusion, firstly, a matter to be taken most seriously by the Trial Chamber in light of the matters covered in the majority Appeals decision and dissenting opinion of Judge Hunt. And I also note Your Honours observations from the Trial Chamber in Galic in that regard. But leaving that aside, acts and conduct of the accused, surrounding circumstances, interests of justice, late notification of this particular witness and the effect that that has in relation to the Defence situation, and the general scheduling of the ability of the Defence to deal with the Prosecution case. Those are my submissions, Your Honours, and -- unless there are any further specific matters Your Honour wishes know go to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Loukas. Mr. Hannis, would you please respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. With regard to late notification, Your Honour, when we field our witness list in December 2003 we indicated at that time that there were something in the neighbourhood of, I think, eight or ten witnesses that we were considering once we were able to speak with them and determine whether or not they would be available. This is one of those witnesses, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think, as a matter of fact, that Ms. Loukas was not complaining about not announcing that such a witness came, but of course it's difficult to prepare if you don't know who it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think that's the issue raised by Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: That's precisely correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the reason that we couldn't do that, Your Honour, was that this witness was not permitted to speak to us until a waiver was brought from Serbia and that was pending for almost two years before we obtained their approval. With regard to the argument about the -- the appropriateness of Rule 89(F), Your Honour, Rule 89(F) says that "The Chamber may receive evidence of a witness where the interests of justice allow in written form." We would contend that the interests of justice would allow those portions of his written statement that I propose in this case. I have gone through and in every instance that I could find where there was mention of the acts and conduct of the accused, I highlighted those for redaction. They have been redacted. I do not propose to submit that evidence regarding this accused in the written form. I will lead that from this witness viva voce. I -- I disagree with the argument that they are not separable. I believe the Court can look at his statement, see what's been redacted, see what remains, and determine whether or not they can be discussed separately. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was there another point you wished me to address, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There's one issue, that is, where Ms. Loukas says that it doesn't save time because she'll need anyhow the weekend to prepare for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I would submit it does save time because if the Court determines that I'm not permitted to introduce any of his evidence in written form, then I will lead that viva voce and that will be time that we all spend in the courtroom with me asking him questions about all those other un-redacted items in the proposed 89(F) statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you say -- if I understand you correctly, that you say that at least Ms. Loukas gain some time in cross-examination by leading the evidence in the 89(F) matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, whatever time she's given, she would gain that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, is there any need to briefly respond? And take an example of Mr. Hannis, who was quite ...

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Your Honours already made the point that my submissions in relation to the late notification did not go for the reasons on the part of the Prosecution for the late notification but what impact that has in relation to the Defence. Beyond that, Your Honour, the question of reduction of time or what have you, that, of course, I went to in the context of what the Prosecution might put forward to the Trial Chamber as potential reduction of time, that that does not detract from the essence and the substance of the argument, Your Honour, and that is that this sort of evidence, with the numbers of references that the statement has, taking into account the surrounding circumstances, taking into account the acts and conduct of the accused question, this is a matter of substance in applying the discretion -- under 89(F) is simply not a suitable statement or witness for the application of 89(F) and it is not divisible simply because the matters contained within the statement are so interrelated. They are intertwined. They are inextricably intertwined, Your Honour. And when one looks, for example -- if I might take Your Honours to -- I have a copy of the redacted version here. These are not just -- these are sentences in the middle of particular paragraphs throughout the statement as well as entire paragraphs. Your Honours, this is not a matter that one could say in any realistic fashion is divisible. Those are my submissions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Loukas. Ms. Loukas, Mr. Hannis, the Chamber does not find that the statement is indivisible, as you argued, and therefore does not exclude 89(F). Further, the late introduction of this witness does not affect the way in which the evidence through this witness is led. As far as the preparation for cross-examination is concerned, the Chamber does not need to decide that right away, and we'll consider that. Therefore, Mr. Hannis, you may call your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which is --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Milorad Davidovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Usher, would you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, while that's happening --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May I simply introduced -- I didn't earlier because he wasn't here. Michael -- Mr. Michael Matlak, who is now with the Defence team for the next few weeks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Welcome in the court, Mr. Matlak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Davidovic. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is now handed out to you by Madam Usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Davidovic. Please be seated. You'll first be examined by Mr. Hannis, counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'd like to begin by first of all showing this witness two items: His redacted ICTY statement, if that could be given a number; and also, a supplemental information sheet, if that could be given a separate number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you please assign first of all a number to the redacted statement. Madam Registrar, if a number could be assigned.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That would be number P764 and P764A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And as well -- is "A" the supplemental information sheet or is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that "A" is the supplemental information sheet.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, could you please take a look at those two items, the first being a redacted version of your ICTY statement and the second being a supplemental information which contains some of the changes that we made after reviewing it in preparation if your testimony today. First of all, do you recognise your original ICTY statement?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And have you now had a chance to look at the B/C/S version of the supplemental information sheet which contains some of the changes that we made after proofing you for your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And having had a chance to review your statement before coming to court today and having made those changes, are you satisfied with that statement and are you able to certify to the Court that that statement is truthful and accurate to the best of your knowledge and belief?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The statement is correct and truthful, and what I said is properly reflected in this paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: One other item I would like show the witness, Your Honour, would be the next exhibit number, please. This is an intercepts authorisation sheet -- authentication. I'm sorry. Mr. Davidovic, during the course of preparing your statement, you may recall that we played some intercepted telephone conversations for you in which you were able to in some cases make voice identifications and comment on the content of some of those. Can you indicate to us whether or not that document in front of you is the summary of what was done in connection with those intercepted conversations and if it's also true and accurate to the best of your information and belief.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, were copies provided -- a number to the Chamber so that we can have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yeah. It will be P764B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But could we have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. At this point in time, I would like to read an 89(F) summary of what is in the -- in the redacted version of his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, I think counsel is trying to address me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I was trying to do it with some subtlety, Your Honour. On the basis that -- I was wondering when the Prosecutor had actually forwarded the 89(F) summary to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm looking at my case manager. Apparently we haven't.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: That's what I thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I would indicate to counsel, however, the 89(F) summary is almost identical to the information that was provided about this witness at the time we requested that he be added as an additional witness. It's basically a cut and paste from that motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But it's unclear. Has Ms. Loukas received the copy or ...

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I haven't. And the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether -- whether it's cut and paste or -- I mean, Ms. Loukas is entitled to have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. I didn't realise she had not been given a copy this morning. I have an extra.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, since the summaries are mainly meant to inform the public, it's not necessary to read it right away, Ms. Loukas. You can have a -- you take your time to review the summary and see whether there's any comment, and Mr. Hannis would then read that, perhaps after the first break or at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. I think that's an appropriate course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And I just want to ensure that the Prosecution endeavours to ensure that I am sent the 89(F) summaries prior to the witness coming to court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour. I apologise for the oversight on this occasion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I would indicate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would have one question, however: Mr. Hannis, you -- let me just check that on the transcript. Yes. I see it's just -- not just identification but it's also comments on the -- I take it that then you consider this to be also a kind of 89(F) procedure?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour, but I will be leading some viva voce testimony from him concerning the substance of some of those conversations that may pertain to the accused or those close to the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Loukas, you're aware of the comments. Is there any problem in -- of course, apart from your general problem with 89(F) evidence led through this witness, but if there are specific portions on -- especially on the comments. I mean, identification is perhaps a different matter. Then please led us know if Mr. Hannis, in your view, would not pay sufficient attention to the portions that in your view certainly would not be acceptable under 89(F), coming too close to the accused or related to the acts and the conduct of the accused.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would indicate also for the 89(F) summary, I indicated that it was taken from the prior motion. However, one change that was made was I omitted some of the things from the motion that went directly to the acts and conduct of the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Ms. Loukas has an opportunity to review it and you'll hear from her if there's any objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, a little while later on I will read a summary of what's in your redacted statement, but from this point we'll talk about the fact that your working career was as a professional policeman. And in your statement I think you indicated you started work in 1974, and after various jobs and working various locations you became the chief of police in Bijeljina municipality in 1989. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, are you certain about that? Your statement indicates 1989.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm certain. I was a commander of the traffic police in 1989 in Bijeljina. No. I'm sorry. I do apologise. Yes, 1989. I got confused. You were correct in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I'm going to talk about -- or ask you a question about paragraph 10 in your statement. You talk about the elections in 1990, the -- the multiparty elections. Before the elections actually took place, you mention that you were approached by local SDS members about joining the SDS, and in paragraph 10, you say that they said, "If you're not with us, you're against us." Could you explain what your understanding of that was in regard to the request to join the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Even before the start of the elections, when the SDS party was being set up in Bijeljina, some individuals tried to get me involved in this process, the setting-up of the party. I was not of the view that it was possible for me to do that and to opt for such a political choice, but once the party had already been registered and they started to act officially, then again they tried to attract members. And I always refused. And even when they won the elections, I was asked to join in and I refused once again. And I believe that my understanding of the role of the police and police service with regard to any political parties, that is to say, that it was irreconcilable, was correct. But the way in which it was done and people who were trying to set up the party were really low-level individuals, from my point of view. I knew some of those people. They had suspicious pasts, and in the past they were sometimes involved in crime, and I thought it would be inconceivable for me to join in with these people. But they did say, "If you're not with us, you're against us." And when SDS came to power, a very unpleasant situation arose, in terms of the way in which the members of that political party viewed and interpreted things. They considered that whoever was not a sympathiser or a member of the party was their enemy, whether it was a Serb or a member of any other ethnicity. When I say "Serbs," I mean they normally said if you were a Serb and you were not with them, you were some kind of traitor. You were not real Serbs. And I must admit this is something which I've always failed to understand. I mean, we are second-class Serbs or what? We were not in the same category of the people joining the Serb party.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: And then --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If you could stop you there. I think you've satisfied the answer to that question. Let me ask you, then: After at the recollections and the SDS came to power in Bijeljina, what happened to you and your position in the police department in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: As soon as they came to power, far-reaching changes started and they started getting rid of people, within the judiciary, the police, et cetera, and anything that had to do with implementation of the law. They immediately changed the entire team when it came to the SUP leaders at the local level, the local community level, and the same thing was done at the republic level and at the local level. All the leadership positions were changed and members of other ethnic groups who were leaving the service or trying to go abroad, well, they were leaving these positions vacant and they were filled by their people and then they were also going through the lists of people who are on the reserve lists of the police. And if you were not a sympathiser or a close collaborator of that party, you would be dropped from the police force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. May I ask you to carefully listen to the question and, to start with, to answer the question specifically put to you. The question was: What happened to you? And, of course, it may be that Mr. Hannis is interested also to know what happened to others, but the question was what happened to you. Would you first focus on that. We are under some time restraints. Mr. Davidovic, you'll understand that hearing evidence of what happened in the former Yugoslavia could easily take you four, five, or six years even in one case. We can't do that. So please focus on the specific questions put to you. If more information is needed, Mr. Hannis certainly will ask for it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Davidovic, then what did happen to you in terms of your position as chief in the Bijeljina police station?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I was replaced. New people came along and they took over my role.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who -- who was put in your old position?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Predrag Jesuric. He used to be a lawyer before. And I think he was behind the setting up and the registration of the party and the chief of municipal police was a member of the Bosniak people, a professor who worked at a school. I can't remember his name right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, had Mr. Jesuric had any prior police experience, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when you say he was behind the setting-up and the registration of the party, which party are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: The SDS party. He was leading the party from the very start. He prepared the documents for the registration, and he was one of the key people within the party from the start.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Davidovic, I now want to move to a point later in time. After you had been replaced, you sought employment with the federal SUP, and I'm looking at paragraph 14 of your statement now. Could you explain briefly to the Judges what the -- what the federal SUP is and where that is in the hierarchy of the police organisations in the former Yugoslavia. In particular, how it relates to the republican MUPs and the local SUPs. If you can just do that briefly.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: The federal SUP is based in Belgrade and it is a federal institution which dealt with internal affairs at the level of the former Yugoslavia, and they were in charge of the federal institutions, apart from security forces and any security-related activities, they had a role in coordinating expert coordination amongst MUPs at the republic level, in terms of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In the former Yugoslavia before the war there was only one federal SUP for the entire Yugoslavia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was the federal SUP, the federal police.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then there was a separate republican MUP for each of the republics that were members of Yugoslavia, Croatia, Slovenia, Bosnia, et cetera; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In every republic, depending on the constitutional provisions - I'm talking about the 1974 Constitution - every republic had such a body with full authority for all these matters, and they were in charge of everything. The federal SUP only had an institutional supervision power, in terms of their expert duties. They did not have the right to supervise operational activities except for the secret police.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then within each of the republics, at the municipal -- at the municipality levels, there was a component of the police that was known as the SUP and their physical facilities was the SJB; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. At the republic level, there was a Ministry of the Interior, which consisted of the State Security and Public Security. And then it was republic MUPs, the security offices at the regional level, and then at municipal level.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when the SUPs at the municipal level and the MUP at the republic level, you mentioned regional levels. What were they called? Was there a name or an acronym for them?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were called the centres of the security service. They were called centres. It would be the first step up, starting from the municipal level. So we had to communicate through them, and they were in charge of communicating between us and the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] And you said that -- in paragraph 14, you say that you became -- you became a chief inspector when you joined the federal SUP. How many chief inspectors in the whole of Yugoslavia were there?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Each republic had a chief, and there were five in the police. In Yugoslavia, there weren't more than five or six of us in total.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Davidovic, I want to skip ahead a little bit and go to paragraph 23 of your statement, where you talk about a -- a mission to Bosnia-Herzegovina in September 1991 and you talk about a joint commission that was dealing with issues of police staffing and ethnicity within the police force, relations with the JNA, et cetera. You talk about the first meeting that happened at Han Pijesak in September/October 1991. I want to ask you about a second meeting that you described in paragraph 25 at Banja Luka. Can you tell the Court who attended that meeting in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: In Banja Luka there was Petar Gracanin on behalf of the federal SUP, and I was with him. On behalf of Republika Srpska -- or rather on behalf of Bosnia- Herzegovina, there was Biljana Plavsic, Mr. Koljevic, Kljujic, a member of the Presidency was there, there was Ganic, also a Presidency member. Zepinic was there, the then-chief of the public security station in Banja Luka. There was the commander, Uzelac, a lieutenant colonel. He was a corps commander, the commander of a corps in Banja Luka. And there was Mr. Tirnanic, an assistant in the Federal Ministry for Internal Affairs. He was the assistant of Petar Gracanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can -- can you tell us what was discussed at that meeting with these representatives from the Presidency and the military.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: They discussed the future tasks of the security service and coordination between the army and the police. I think that they continued discussions that had been commenced in Han Pijesak and they tried to reach an agreement according to which the police with the federal SUP would be engaged at joint checkpoints and they would coordinate the work of the police and the army. At these checkpoints the federal SUP police were to be present and the police from the army and from Bosnia and Herzegovina were also to be present there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, may I --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- just ask one question to the witness. You said that "Also present was Mr. Zepinic, the then-chief of the public security station in Banja Luka."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Security Services Centre in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was Mr. Zepinic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Stojan Zepinic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In regard to that, Mr. Davidovic, I would indicate to you that there has been some evidence that the security chief in Banja Luka whose last name was Zupljanin, and there was a Zepinic, who was a member of the federal --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Zupljanin. Zupljanin. I apologise. Please don't tie me down to precise surnames. A long time has passed since then and I'm really not able to remember all the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand we're talking about persons and events from 13 years ago. And in the proofing I know you indicated to me that sometimes with dates and names you have difficulties. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do object to evidence from the bar table in the context of leading evidence from a witness in this way. Firstly, the -- the filling-of-the-gap aspect, I mean, that was the witness's evidence. If it needs to be cleared up later, it can be cleared up later. But -- but secondly, there's some -- you know, "during the proofing session you indicated this." That is thoroughly inappropriate, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, I think that the witness indicated that a long time has passed, and, of course, that's part of his evidence. I asked this question because the Chamber heard quite some evidence about Mr. Zupljanin being the -- in the position where the witness did put Mr. Zepinic ... I think that reference to what happened during the proofing session, especially in this respect, is not -- is not necessary and could better be avoided.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will try to do that in the future, Your Honour. I was trying to indicate that that is something that you will see -- partly from the corrections that are made in the supplemental information, you will see that names have been changed and dates have been changed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And he has indicated that on more than one occasion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, now I want to go to paragraph 30 of your statement, and you explain your statement a little bit about what the commission was trying to do and one of the things you did was examining -- examine what was happening in Bosnia with regard to the police force and the number of reserve police and the arming of the reserve police. You mention that -- you talk about an example in Tuzla municipality where the number of reserve police apparently had been greatly increased to approximately 10.000. I want to quote a line from your statement. You say: "The new SDS Bijeljina chief refused to surrender these weapons," referring to some 900 weapons, "that the Tuzla chief was requesting be returned because he had made a change in -- or a reduction in the number of reserve police." At that time, in Bijeljina who was the chief?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the time Predrag Jesuric was the chief of police. To go back to what you asked me about earlier on, as a commission it was our task to establish whether the Security Services had acted on reports filed by citizens with regard to clashes on an ethnic basis. They had to decide whether there had been any reports concerning the army and the police and citizens, and we had to establish whether the police and the reserve police force had applied the law. We had to decide how the reserve force functioned, what its ethnic composition was, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in your statement, you indicate that -- that all three of the national parties were engaged in this process of trying to arm their groups by increasing the number of reserve police in those municipalities where they were a majority. Does that apply to Croats, Serbs, and Muslims equally? Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to ask you another question related to -- to arming of the civilian population, and I'm going now to paragraphs 39 to 41 of your statement, not necessarily just civilians but others as well. You describe in your paragraphs how weapons and equipment were transferred from the Republic of Serbia in Belgrade to the newly formed Republika Srpska. Paragraph 39, the last sentence, you talk about high-quality weapons for approximately 500 men. What kind of weapons were you talking about there when you say "high-quality weapons"

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Infantry weapons on the whole, automatic weapons. There were some Heckler weapons. There were weapons for special purposes, with silencers, et cetera, and there were new NATO rifles, rifles used by the NATO forces at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned in paragraph 40 about weapons and equipment going on to helicopters for transport to Pale. Whose helicopters were these? What agency or organisation had helicopters for this purpose?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, these were the Yugoslav Army's helicopters, JNA helicopters. We would take the weapons to the airport at Batajnica or to the barracks in Bajnica and the weapons were then transferred to Republika Srpska, or rather, to Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You talk about going on the first occasion with Pero Mihajlovic when some weapons and equipment were actually handed over. First of all, tell me who was Pero Mihajlovic.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Pero Mihajlovic went with me when I went to Pale for the first time. He was a member of the federal SUP. He worked in the Department for Foreigners and for Passports. I think that was the name of the department. He was in charge of those weapons because I gave him the weapons from the brigade. I couldn't take those weapons and give them to him. I had to assign this task to someone, who would then hand these weapons over to him. He was a colleague of mine from the federal SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And on this trip that you went with him to hand over weapons and equipment, do you recall how much equipment? What was the quantity of equipment and weapons you delivered on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we went there by helicopter on the first occasion. We only took uniforms, flak jackets, some helmets, some field boots. This is equipment from the special unit of our brigade, and that is the equipment that we took with us on that first occasion. We did not take any weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Because it was too heavy. We couldn't carry more than that with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who ordered that and directed you to take the equipment on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: The federal minister, Kalipovic [phoen], who issued the order, and there was a request from the assistant minister, Kertes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And that was -- that was the federal minister of which agency?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: The federal Ministry of Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I want to back up for just a second because when we started a discussion about arming, I had asked you a question about Mr. Jesuric as the Bijeljina chief who refused to surrender weapons. I would like to show you just one shot from a video.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is a video that's already in evidence, Your Honour. It's a -- it's an interview on a TV programme called "My Guest - His Truth."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, did you know an individual named Mirko Blagojevic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He's someone from Bijeljina. I knew him from before the war, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who was he and was he associated with any political party or any group in Bijeljina at the -- in late 1991 and early 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mirko Blagojevic was the first associate of Mr. Seselj's. He was a member of the Radical Party. When this party was first established, Mirko Blagojevic was its secretary, and I think that he was even its president for a certain period of time. But he was a secretary of the party on a permanent basis and he was one of Seselj's key associates.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you also know an individual by the name of Branislav Filipovic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Brano Filipovic is a criminal who was convicted on a number of occasions. But when the war broke out, he immediately joined Mirko Blagojevic and the Radicals, and he was one of the key individuals involved in the clashes at the beginning of the war and right up until the time that he was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to show you a copy of the transcript of a TV interview. Do you recall having seen a video during proofing of Mirko Blagojevic talking about his experiences during the war?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, you indicated that this was a video which is already in evidence. Could you please tell us under what number.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the number is P727, and it's in the Brcko dossier at tab 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, I'm sorry, Mr. Davidovic, I don't know where we left off. Did you -- did you -- you recall seeing that video?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I've handed you the transcript, and it's page 19 of the English, Your Honour. And in the B/C/S, Mr. Davidovic, I think it's on page 17. The time counter is at 2 hours, 50 minutes, and 29 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I have it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Is that the -- the Branislav Filipovic referred to there, is that the one you knew in Bijeljina that you have been talking about?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did he have a nickname that you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: They called him Sumar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'd like to hand him another item which should get the next exhibit number, please. And this is a document dated the 31st of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, could you tell us what that document is.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The next exhibit number will be P765.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is a travel order that is issued to individuals using an army vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was Mr. Filipovic a member of the regular army in 1991 or 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No. He was a member of the Radical Party. They had an armed formation which was engaged in the Brcko area at the beginning of the war. That is where they were. They had their headquarters and their forces, their men and equipment there. They were engaged in operations in the Brcko area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I have nothing further to ask you about that document at this time, sir. I want to go to another topic in your statement, that's the first paragraph under the heading about "Assistance to the new Republika Srpska MUP," and you talk about around April 6th, 1992 you were called in to see Kertes and Gracanin. Do you recall that meeting; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Would you tell the Judges, please, what happened at that meeting? What did they talk about? What did they tell you they wanted you to do?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I was summoned to the meeting by Mr. Kertes. He asked me to come to the ministry, and that's why I saw Kertes and the minister. The minister was Petar Gracanin at the time. Kertes then told me -- he asked me, "What are you doing here? Why aren't you in Bosnia? Do you want me to defend the Serbs in Bosnia given that I'm a Hungarian?" He asked me to engage as many men as I could and to go to Bosnia and help the Serbian people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did -- was this a request?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It wasn't a request, but he then asked for a solution to be found, for me to go there immediately. I asked him how I was to go there. He said, "We'll find a way for you to go there but you'll be a member of the federal SUP. You'll remain a member of the federal SUP but whatever you do there will be done under the auspices of the Republika Srpska." I wanted this to be legally regulated. I wanted there to be a decision because if I was killed, I wanted to -- it to be clear what my status was. They then called Marko Baletic, who was the secretary in the federal SUP at the time and he was told that he should prepare the necessary documents and issue decisions according to which we were going on leave, but we were to leave our official documents in the federal SUP and take those decisions with us. And when we arrived in the republican MUP, we would receive other documents, decisions stating that we were policemen there and that we could work there, but any additional salaries, any additional remuneration was to be paid out to us in the federal MUP. I remember one detail: Marko Baletic said, "How are we going to do this? This isn't legal." And Kertes reacted very angrily, even brazenly. He said, "What kind of law are you talking about?" I'll say this quite freely. He said, "Fuck the law. Do whatever I say. There's no other law." And Marko had no other comments. He said, "Okay, that's what we'll do. That's how we'll proceed," and that's what we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me try and clear this up. At the beginning, I asked you whether Kertes's remark to you about going to the Republika Srpska to help defend it, was that a request that you felt you could refuse?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think that it's the right of every man to say whether he will go or not, but the request was quite decisive. He said, "You're going to Bosnia. What are you doing here in Brdo [as interpreted]? Do you want me as a Hungarian to defend the people?" That meant that I had to go there. That is what was implied.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that Mr. Gracanin was the -- the Minister of the Interior at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... your direct supervisor, your boss?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then what was Mr. Kertes's position in relation to Gracanin and in relation to you in the -- in the hierarchy, in the structure, in the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gracanin was the federal secretary. He was a minister. He was the main person. But when Kertes arrived as an assistant, he took decisions on behalf of the secretariat. Petar Gracanin wasn't asked much about such details, and Gracanin always gave in to Kertes. Kertes imposed himself. He had been sent from Republika Srpska to work in the federal SUP. And there's something I have to say. He was sent there to break up the federal SUP. They still thought that we were the former Yugoslav SUP composed of men from various ethnic groups. There were men from other republics there, and they thought that we in the federal SUP were against the future activities that the forces in Bosnia and Herzegovina would be involved in, and we were against the way in which they were going to deal with the state of the Serbs in the upcoming war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And so they treated us in a somewhat unusual way and they always viewed us slightly condescendingly, as an organisation opposed to the policies of Slobodan Milosevic. Those policies were quite nationalistic. Kertes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, let me stop you there. You were talking about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, if you would allow me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to seek one clarification. Witness, you said -- at least, that's what I read on the transcript: "And when we arrived in the republican MUP, we would receive other documents, decisions stating that we are policemen there and that we could work there, but any additional salaries, any additional remuneration was to be paid out to us in the federal MUP"; whereas, until now, at the federal level you referred, rather, to the SUP than to the MUP. Could you explain here why any additional remuneration was to be paid out to you in the federal MUP.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know how clearer I can be. The federal MUP is the federal MUP and the republican MUP is at the level of the republic. These are the same institutions. But I worked in the federal SUP. I continue to work for that SUP. I had a right to a salary there. But when I went to Bosnia, I only received fabricated documents in case I was killed somewhere, in case I or one of my men were arrested or killed, we needed such documents to confirm that we were not from Yugoslavia but that we were, in fact, members of the Republika Srpska MUP. So this -- the purpose of these documents was to conceal our actual identity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm -- I do understand that part of your testimony. I do not fully understand why any additional payment would come from the federal MUP rather than from the federal SUP.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. The federal MUP and the federal SUP, well, it's the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Until now, you used the -- usually the abbreviation "federal SUP." I do understand that the difference is "SUP" stands for secretariat and MUP stands for ministry. So you say that's the same. Then I better understand your testimony. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That helped clear up my confusion as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So -- now I want to ask you about your answer where you indicated that Mr. Kertes had been sent to -- to break things up. Who sent him?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic. Prior to that, Mr. Kertes was a member of the Presidency of the Republic of Serbia. He was a member of the Presidency of that body that was the leading body at the level of the Republic of Serbia and it was considered that the federal SUP -- that federal ministry, that is. We've got several different words, secretariat or what have you, but it's all the same. It was considered that it was still a bastion of resistance to the policies of Mr. Milosevic. It was considered somebody stronger than Mr. Petar Gracanin as a general could be placed in that position who would be more skilled and would be more able to introduce rigorous changes and break it up, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in that earlier answer, you said "they didn't like" -- I don't recall your exact words. They didn't like the federal SUP because you were sort of a multi-ethnic group and not in favour of the nationalistic policies. Who was the "they" that they were referring to in that answer?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely what I mean is the Republic of Serbia and people who were leading figures at the level of the Republic of Serbia, the policies of Mr. Milosevic, and Mr. Kertes as one of the represents of that policy.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. In this meeting, when it was discussed how logistically you were going to be able to go to the Republika Srpska, you mentioned that Mr. Baletic objected and said it would be illegal. Did he explain why in his opinion it would be illegal?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: He said that it was against the law for a simple reason, because an employee of the federal ministry -- of the federal MUP, that is, could not simply go and work for the SUP at the level of the republic and use their equipment and bear their insignia or what have you. It was illogical for somebody working at the state level, federal level, and -- to go and work at the republic -- at the level of the republic. We couldn't work for them and continue to receive our salaries back in Belgrade. So there were different legal provisions in terms of organising contracts, et cetera. So we were talking about two different categories, different budget lines, different funding, everything. And that's why he couldn't find a solution. How could he send us to work there officially on a business trip, as it were? And that's why he said there was no legal basis for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Judge Hanoteau as a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to ask the following question: Why, in your view, did they contact you and what do you think they expected you to do? Why did they choose you in particular and what was the kind of mission that you were entrusted [Realtime transcript read in error "interested"] interested with down there?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "Entrusted with," not "interested."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was a high-ranking official within the federal SUP. I was the chief police inspector and it was the highest ranking position at that time, in terms of anyone from Bosnia and Herzegovina working within the federal SUP, and it was only logical that as such a highest ranking official I would have been asked to gather people from Bosnia around me and go to Bosnia. It was obvious. It went without saying. So it was not something that was put anywhere in writing, but the armed forces asked for people who were originally from Bosnia to go to Bosnia, and the same happened within SUP. And I was the highest ranking Bosnian official, so I was asked to go and organise things there.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm just wondering if it would be possible to take the break at 10.25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had not finished with my questions. In the reply you gave, did you mean to say that you were being sent down there because you were the highest ranking official but also because you had the highest qualifications? You were asked to get other people organised.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Well, I had spent a long time within the police force. I was a professional policeman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, it's still 10.25. There must be specific reason why you asked for a break.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: This is an urgent matter, Your Honour, that's just arisen. And I do apologise to Judge Hanoteau. I thought he'd finished asking his questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll then have an early break, Mr. Hannis, if you do not disagree. We'll adjourn until ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I ask you one brief question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Very shortly I intend to play some intercepted conversations. Most of these that I have are ones that are on the intercept authentication sheet, which he's listened to and made his comments in terms of identifying voices and something about the content. Because in my view some of that content seemed to relate to matters that -- not necessarily acts and conduct of the accused but the acts and conduct of some individuals closely associated with him or high ranks. For purposes of 89(F), I thought this was material that I needed to leave --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You should say it's too much in the proximity of the accused to introduce them in any other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. But I didn't know if the Court wanted me to play the entire intercept or if I could go to portions in the transcript or if Ms. Loukas had an objection to either process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, if you'd play only portions of it, the Chamber is not immediately in a position to see whether that would cause any specific problem. Ms. Loukas might be in a position. If she thinks that it's appropriate to have the whole context of the conversation in evidence as well, we'll hear from her. But let's start with playing those portions that are in the view of the Prosecution most relevant.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. Just one first matter that I might indicate prior to the witness being brought into court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: There is just an introduction I would like to make to the Court, and that is that Mr. David Josse is with us today, who's recently been appointed a legal consultant in relation to the Defence team and hopefully will be able to join the Defence team should we continue as Mr. Krajisnik's representatives in light of his application to represent himself as co-counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I might spend a few more words on it later today. But first of all, welcome in this courtroom, Mr. Josse. Then if there's nothing else, then, Mr. Hannis, I'll ask Madam Usher to escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, before we continue, I should indicate to you that the interpreters spoke to me during the break and indicated that I've been guilty sometimes in the past of speaking too fast, and I know they indicate that you speak rapidly sometimes. They also indicated that sometimes your enunciation combined with the speed made it difficult for them. So please bear that in mind. I wanted to ask you -- we were talking about the meeting you had with Kertes and Gracanin where it was decided for you to go to Republika Srpska. In paragraph 44 of your statement, you say: "The problem was the federal SUP could not be seen to be taking sides with the RS MUP." Why not? What was the problem with that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was not supposed to appear as a country participating in war, so it was a war but it was taking place outside the official bodies within that country.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did anyone tell you that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, no. It went without saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, I want to play an intercepted telephone conversation for you that -- that you have heard before and actually made comments on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we can give this a number. This is a conversation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, it will be P766.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, I would tell you this is from approximately the 18th of April, 1992. We'll listen to it all the way through and then I'll have some questions for you at the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, it would not appear on the transcript if it's not read by the interpreters. It will then also not appear on the French transcript. So could you please restart and could I invite, according to our usual procedure, to ask one of the interpreters to read it and the other one to follow it on paper. And we are aware that the speed is such that the interpreter reading the English text will be behind, but we'll just in this way verify that everything is consistent both on paper and in audio. Could we restart, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Yes. Good afternoon. Good afternoon. Is this Pero? Yes. This is Sarajevo here. Hold on a moment. Cedo Kljajic needs to speak to you. Thank you. Hello? Yes. Hello. Hi. How are you? What's going on? What's up, Pero? Fuck, all kinds of things. I've been working. When are you going to how many here, man? Look, I told Dragan, but I don't know if he managed to convey it on to you. Here we've reached an agreement. Kijac? Yes. All right. He did tell us. Yes. We've agreed that this should go through these colleagues from this Ministry next door. Mm-hm. So I don't appear in the official procedure any more. All right. I thought I could come for a private visit. But won't you be coming here any more? Well, no. Why not? Well, the ministers, this federal one, and the Serb minister from next door have decided this cooperation should go through them in the future. Oh, damn. Fuck, I don't know. Maybe if somebody ... that's why I wanted to talk to you. All right. That's one thing. The other thing is ... What can we do so that I can reach agreement with Mico? He's for any solution that can contribute to ... We can't really make any arrangements on the phone. I was hoping one of you would come here so that we... We, too, wanted to come. We've tried to insist on that, but you know how it is. Problems arise one after another and that has slowed down everything. I can see you have a whole lot of problems. Yes. And that ... it is very complicated. Here we had reached an agreement, designated some to send, but I had organised it all. I was going to transport it to you but I ... didn't work out. This is why it is all going through the colleagues from the next door who will ... Yes. Yes. That's one thing. The other thing ... when he called ... that I have Momo here. I couldn't get through ... Momo ordered some equipment from our institute of security. All right. Well, you know what was still functioning and we have now stopped it all. Yeah. We don't want it to go to these guys. Momo didn't order that for the Serb MUP but for that ... Yes. Yes. So we stop all that. Sure. All of it. I will ... because they called me. I will stop it all now. Well, if you could bring that to us here, we could make further arrangements, you know. Fuck, we need to get together. Maybe we could do that. I'm going to check that now. Can you bring it about then? I can't. Not even that? It was said that -- Listen, Pero ... Can you come here for a private visit? Well, today I can't ... we'll see, but not today. I'll check if I can come one of these days for a private visit. If I don't come, I could send that Mico Davidovic from here, the one you know, on a Saturday or Sunday. Yeah, I know him. Maybe him then. I'd prefer if you came. Well, I'd like to come but ... Let him come too, but I'd prefer it if you came, you know. All right. We could also arrange some other things, some relations, you know. Yes. Yes, we should. I'll wait today. There are helicopters flying from Belgrade and here daily. I can't reach him, damn it. You should ask around. They're operating constantly, you know? It would help if Mico called and said. Who does he need to arrange this with? My boss, Gracanin. All right. I just received what you had sent to me and it is very interesting. It has drawn serious attention. Mm-hm. Here, I mean. Yeah. I could make an arrangement with him. All right. Hey, do you know if ... some of my people from Semberija and Majevica had a talk on personnel issues last night. Have you determined who will be the mayor of Bijeljina? No. I did talk to Jasaric but we discussed another issue. Yes. No, they didn't ... All right. There were some people here last night but I don't know if they were at your place or somewhere else ... They were probably up there. Yeah, up there. Pero, please, come for a private visit, if you can. I'm try and you can check it with Mico then. Yeah, I'll do the rest with Mico. Maybe you could have Mico talk to you ... if I can't come now. Give me a call if you can't make it. I'll know whether I can or not today. I'll let you know. Check that today and call me immediately. You got it. All right. You go got it. I'll give you a call if I can't make it, and then you reply ... Exactly. You got it. There. Bye. I'll talk to you later. Talk to you later. Cheers. Bye.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we have not finished the French translation. I'm -- we're still at the helicopters. Could the French translators continue and finish their ... I'm not quite sure I understood, which seemed to be a request for an additional ten minutes by the French interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Quite some time. So perhaps we could add the transcript of the translation later so as not to waste any more time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It might be -- it might be difficult to insert at a later stage the missing portion, so even if it takes time, I would highly appreciate if the translation would be finished right away. And I take it that the interpreters have the English text in front of them. Yes. So I invite the French interpreters to finish the translation. Please proceed, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, did you recognise the speakers in that conversation?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who were they?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Pero Mihajlovic, my colleague from the federal SUP, and Cedo Kljajic, who at the time was an assistant to the Ministry -- minister of the interior for public security.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Early in the conversation, Mr. Mihajlovic had made a remark about, "We've agreed that this should go through the colleagues from the ministry next door." In the context of that conversation, and knowing who Mr. Mihajlovic was, do you know what he's referring to there, what ministry next door?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. A building, the Federal Ministry of the Interior, was across the road from the Republic of Serbia's ministry, so we were divided by this street. And when he says "next door," or "across the road," what he meant, it would be within the area of competence of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And just shortly after that he says, "The ministers, this federal one, and the Serb minister from next door, have decided this cooperation should go through them in the future." The federal one would be who?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Not through them but that all future cooperation with the MUP of the Republic -- of the Republika Srpska should go through the MUP of the Republic of Serbia, no longer through the federal ministry. The federal ministry should be out of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Who was the federal one that they're referring, to the federal minister, the name of that person?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Petar Gracanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the Serb minister from next door, who would that have been in April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Sokolovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, your name is mentioned in that conversation. But near the end, Mr. Mihajlovic is asking Cedo Kljajic, "Have you determined who will be the mayor of Bijeljina yet?" Do you remember hearing that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, not the mayor but the chief of MUP in Bijeljina. He said that Cedo didn't know. The way I understood, it was about MUP because afterwards, very soon afterwards Predrag Jesuric was replaced by another man, and Predrag Jesuric was moved to another job within the Ministry of the Republika Srpska, within the Ministry of the Interior, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Maybe there is a problem in my translation. My English has it as "have you determined who will be the major of Bijeljina?" Could you look -- do you have a copy of the B/C/S transcript for this conversation on the table?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be provided with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's the semi-last page --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. It's the page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The ninth -- approximately the ninth box from the top, the first one being empty.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The page number at the top, the last four digits is 0232 and it's Mr. Mihajlovic speaking in the eighth box down with -- that has anything in it. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you read that last sentence in the box. It talks about Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I still think -- "Have you decided who would be the chief at Bijeljina?" So the reference is not to the mayor but the chief. And since we are talking here about two people having a conversation and they work for the police, they always mean the police. I don't think he asked the question about the mayor. It is within the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That makes sense to me, Your Honour. I think we would submit a revised translation and change "mayor" to chief. Or if Defence counsel is willing to do it now, perhaps we can do it on the record and I can submit a copy to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Loukas, would there be any problem to do it on the record?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. That seems eminently sensible in the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would then -- I would like to have the original. I'll change that with handwriting and -- so that it reads "chief" rather than "mayor."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, in connection with that, Mr. Kljajic says, "I did talk to Jasaric about that." Do you know who he's referring to there?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Jesuric?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. Do you know who that person was?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: He meant Predrag Jesuric, who was the chief of MUP or SUP in Bijeljina, at the municipal level in Bijeljina.
