utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I understood his name was spelled with a "U," as "Jesuric." This appears in the transcript as Jasaric, with an "A." I think that's just a mispronunciation?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yeah, it's a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And then finally near the end, Mr. Mihajlovic says he will check with Mico and Cedo Kljajic -- no, Pero says, "You should check it with Mico." Cedo Kljajic says he will. What Mico are they talking about? Is that you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No. It was Mico Stanisic. He said, "Should I talk to Mico? Will you?" And then he said, "No, I'll talk to him. So they meant Mico Stanisic, who was the minister the interior of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all I wanted to ask you about for now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And for the benefit of the registry officer, I'm not going to use the next intercept that was on her list, but I would like to go to the following one, which is from the 6th of May. If -- if we could give that a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. It will be P767.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what I propose to do here, Your Honour, is because it's rather long, and I just want it for a point of sort of establishing a date when a certain event happened. I would propose just to ask Mr. Davidovic about a particular passage in the transcript. And if Defence counsel wants to have the whole tape played, then we can do that after -- after I've done that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll hear from Ms. Loukas if she objects.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, this is a conversation between Pero Mihajlovic, and in your authentication sheet I think you identified a second speaker as being Petar Gracanin. But what I'm interested in is on the first page, after the introductory conversations. And it begins at the very bottom of your page in B/C/S, where Mr. Mihajlovic is speaking. Could you read that out for us. It's after he's asked, "Have you arrived?"

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. "Here I am at Vrace, at the headquarters of the Ministry of -- Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I'm at the minister's office. We arrived yesterday. We couldn't return last night. Mico Davidovic, deputy commander of the brigade, is with me."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you read the next three boxes.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: "Mico?" "Yes. We couldn't see it yesterday, since the helicopter by which we came had some other assignment. We couldn't return yesterday. We expect to return during the day, and the minister will probably return too." "Yes. All right."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you recall how many times you went to Pale in a helicopter -- or to -- to the Republika Srpska in a helicopter with Mr. Mihajlovic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I went there with Mihajlovic on two occasions. We went there by helicopter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall being in Vrace with him on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: On the first occasion, we were with him in Vrace. We were in the minister's office and spoke to people there, the people who were in the ministry. I think that Momcilo Mandic was there, too. He was there on the first occasion that we were there. And we spoke about it -- about how to continue sending weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And did this trip occur before you came to Republika Srpska with your group of men to help, as had been proposed by Mr. Kertes?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, these were preparations for my visit to Vrace.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Thank you. That's all I have to ask you about that one.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Just in relation to the last intercept, Your Honours, I can indicate that the Defence has no desire to have the entire intercept played.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The we have a number already? Yes, we have.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, in relation to that I want to ask you about paragraph 46 of your statement. You mentioned that your group arrived in early April; however, in the intercept we just played, which is dated from the first week in May, 1992, it appears that was a preparatory trip you made. So having heard that now, do you still contend that you arrived with your group in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would like the Chamber and the Prosecutor to understand my testimony. I can't remember all the details, all the dates. I was involved in a lot of activities, and I can't remember whether I went there at the beginning of the month or at the end of the month. You must understand that it's been 13 years since I had this conversation. It's very difficult to remember whether this took place at the beginning or at the end of the month, and this is something I've already told the Prosecutor. It's something you have to understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I'm -- I do understand, and I'm hoping that the documents and -- and intercepts will help us firm up dates where we can. In paragraph 46, you talk about when you did arrive with your -- your group of men from the federal SUP, and you met with Stanisic and Mandic at Vrace. You said you asked Stanisic what your task would be. What did Mico Stanisic tell you your tasks were going to be?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, to organise the tasks of the unit for special purposes. This was the special unit that had separated from the former joint republican police. It was to be brought up to strength with new men and we were to create an efficient unit for special purposes. That concerned the organisation of the work in the Republika Srpska ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Before we proceed any further, just as a marker, Your Honours, that question at the end of page 52, I would ask that Mr. Hannis attempt to refrain from comment. "Thank you. I do understand and I'm hoping," what have you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Hannis, to be quite honest, it came into my mind to say something of this kind to you when you said that you understood; whereas the witness, I think, asked the Chamber for understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. I note the marker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, now I want to play another intercept for you. This is -- this is a short one. This is from the 17th of May, 1992. You've heard it before and remark upon it in your intercepts authentication document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could that be given a number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit number P768.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when we're ready, we'll begin that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Hi. Ceca is here. Good evening. Good evening. Is Davidovic there. One moment please. Thank you. Hello. Davidovic? Yes. Ceca is here. Good evening. Good evening. How are you? Good. And you? Very well. Thank you. Here you are, Mile. Thank you. Hello. Yes. How are you, sir? Good. And you? What are you doing? Here I am standing with these people. We are talking a little. I see. Are there any problems? No problems at all. Say hello to the guys. I will. Thank you. If you have time tomorrow, maybe you can pay us a visit. I was just thinking about that. These men went up to Pale. Today we visited the area where we have a separation line, where we will be engaged, so the men can get acquainted, to feel it. Excellent. It would be best for us to meet tomorrow in this -- Excellent. To get to know each other better. Excellent. Thank you. Do you need anything? No. We've got everything. I didn't want to come to bother you, as you are very busy. When I need something, I will contact you through Cedo or maybe I'll do it through you. If I get a chance. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, do you recognise the speakers in that conversation? If so, tell us who they were.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Myself and Mico Stanisic, the Minister of Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what -- what had happened at that time? Can you tell us if this was before or after -- or at the time that you came to Republika Srpska with your group of men from the federal SUP.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: This was when I had arrived in Pale with that group of people. During that period of time, I found accommodation. I went to the secondary school building of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Vrace. We had accommodation in the school building, in the lower part of the building, beneath the classrooms where there were office premises, offices for the teachers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In your statement at paragraph 51, you mentioned while you were at Vrace you saw a unit of Red Berets arrive. You mentioned a person known as "Carli." Where were these Red Berets from?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I then met those people. I met someone who said his name was Carli. He was the commander of the Red Berets. They had come from Serbian. They'd been sent there by the Republican Ministry of the Interior and all the equipment that they had was new, high-quality equipment. They had personal weapons, infantry weapons, and they had official identity cards from the Serbian MUP. The appearance of these individuals and the way they acted was quite interesting. Mostly they had tattoos, they had a particular way of speaking, and this enabled one to identify them as individuals who had the past -- a criminal past. Later I had the opportunity of getting to know some of these people. I could answer some questions if you have any questions you would like to put to me about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I do have a couple more questions. What -- what kind of unit was this? Is this a military unit, a police unit?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: They were a police unit. They had police uniforms, camouflage uniforms, a police insignia, and they introduced themselves as special forces from the Serbian MUP, as special police forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were they -- well, at that time in Yugoslavia, how did one get to be a police officer? Did you have to go to any special kind of school or training?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before someone became a policeman, before the war broke out, in order to become a policeman it was necessary to have finished secondary school, to have served in the army, and to be fit to work in the police force. That meant that you had no criminal record and that you had no tendencies that would place you in the category of individuals who were prone to certain deviations. And what I have in mind is criminal activity. They -- once they're accepted, they're sent to a course, to attend a course, which lasts for at least six months. After the course has been completed, they're trained in some of the republics, sent to certain bodies where they're trainees for about a year. They're trained by a senior policeman, and after one year, these individuals are then appointed to police posts. They can start operating independently as policemen. That is how one proceeded. But when the war broke out, men would join the police overnight. You just put a uniform on and you'd become a policeman overnight. But in these units that were sent from Serbia in particular, well, it wasn't that easy to assemble the men who would be sent to the front line and who would carry weapons. There was a particular procedure that had to be followed. I assume that people with criminal backgrounds were recruited. I know that they would release people from penal and correctional facilities so they could go to the front and they were trained for three or five days and would then become members of a police unit which would be sent to the front or to provide assistance in Republika Srpska. And there is something that is quite interesting that I would like to point out. I have to admit that when these units appeared, I realised that the police force as such could no longer function. It no longer existed. I saw people in -- wearing uniforms like the uniform I wore and had the insignia that I had, but in order to have the uniform I had and wear the insignia I had, well, it's impossible for someone to get a uniform overnight. I'm just making a comparison with those people who were wearing those uniforms. And later in Bijeljina and elsewhere, I saw individuals in police uniforms, high-ranking individuals, et cetera. And this demonstrates the kind -- what kind of people came to work in the MUP and in the police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Let me ask you a question about that. You said earlier that the problem was the federal SUP could not be seen to be taking sides with the RS MUP. Was there any problem with the Republic of Serbia MUP being seen to be taking sides with the RS MUP or the Republika Srpska, period?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I must admit that I didn't notice that that the republican Serbian MUP was involved. They didn't conceal their engagement, in fact. They didn't conceal the engagement of their leaders. I knew them from Belgrade. I had regular contact with them. I didn't notice that they kept this secret. When -- in fact, when they did arrive, they would say that they were from the Serbian MUP. No one tried to conceal this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, for the record, on page 58, line 12, it reads "RS MUP," and that's what you said. But there you had in mind Republic of Serbia MUP; whereas, later you are again referring to RS MUP but then you had something different in mind, and you added to that Republika Srpska. Could you please clarify that, because otherwise it might be quite confusing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay, Your Honour. I -- what I meant when I asked that question was he had earlier said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- And it's in, I think, paragraph --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Just in relation to this, I think it's -- if there is going to be a clarification, in light of the fact that the witness has answered that question, confusing as it may be, it's not appropriate, I think, for the -- for the witness to hear what Mr. Hannis --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: -- was attempting to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, what he was attempting to do is -- what I would like to verify - and I think there's no problem with the witness hearing that; it is even an advantage - to ask Mr. Hannis exactly what he meant when he for the first time said "RS MUP" and then what he meant when he said for the second time "RS MUP." No further clarification is needed. Just to see whether the witness answered the question as it was intended to be put to him by Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, indeed, Your Honour. I take that point. But nevertheless I think Mr. Hannis should be cautioned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: -- not to, in answering Your Honour's question, give the witness any guidance as to how the question might be -- how Mr. Hannis is hoping that the question might be answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Hannis, without giving any further clarifications as to your intention, could you please tell us what you intended to ask the witness and then we'll then verify whether that's how the witness understood it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'll try to do that, Your Honour. I -- I thought I understood him, but I think the understanding was between me and Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In paragraph 44 of your statement, Mr. Davidovic - and we talked about this earlier, in terms of you and a unit from the federal SUP going to the Republika Srpska to help in the fight - you said "The problem was the federal SUP could not be seen to be taking sides with the RS MUP," meaning the federal police agency couldn't go into one of the republics to help one side against another; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Then in -- when you were at Vrace, you saw this unit of Red Berets who had identity cards from the Republic of Serbia MUP. Now they're in the Republika Srpska helping Republika Srpska. Was there a problem with that, with one republic MUP helping another republic MUP?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think that was a problem. They did not conceal their identity at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The matter has been sufficiently clarified. Please proceed, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned in your statement that there was a young woman who was some sort of coordinator for this group of Red Berets and that she introduced herself as being from the Serbian DB. Can you tell the Judges what the Serbian DB was and what relationship it had with the Republic of Serbia MUP.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was a woman there who said she was a coordinator. She was a coordinator. She coordinated between that unit and the State Security Service. And on one occasion I even asked her whether she was from the Serbian MUP and she said, "Yes, I am from the SDB." That means the State Security Service. That's the secret police. And Jovica Stanisic was in charge of it. And she represented that service and worked as a coordinator. She coordinated matters between the Serbian MUP and the Republika Srpska MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in paragraph 53 of your statement, you indicated that you informed your boss, Mr. Gracanin, about chaos and a general disorder and that she gave you some instructions to locate General Mladic. At this time I'd like to play another intercepted conversation, Your Honour, if I may. If we could give it a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is from the 19th of May.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P769.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, I am informed that the French booth has not received the text of this intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It is ERN 0212-9514 through 9519. It's the ET number of the ERN. I think on the English it says "Conversation led on 00.05.1992." It may have been misled by my mentioning the 19th of May. Between Petar Gracanin and Mico Stanisic. Can we confirm whether they have it or not? If not, we'll try and find another copy to give to them.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The English booth do have a copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that the French interpreters have -- have retrieved the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll try and play that now, then. Your Honour, it appears we're having some technical difficulties. What I would like to do then is just hand the witness the transcript and ask him about a particular reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see that the last attempt to have it played was not successful. Please proceed as you intend.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. -- for the Court and counsel I'm going to the English version, page 4, coming up from the bottom, where there is a mention of "Davidovic" by Mr. Gracanin. And I'm not sure where that is in the B/C/S transcript, Mr. Davidovic, but I think it's the first place where your name appears. It's about a page and a half from the end, if you're working from the back to the front.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is on the semi-last page, second box from the top, last three digits, ERN 518, where the question mark appears and -- is that correct, Mr.--

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it the first time where the name appears?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you see that, Mr. Davidovic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the next comment Mr. Gracanin says is "let him wait for you there and let him just say that I sent him." Do you know what he's talking about there?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Before I went to Sarajevo, I was told that whatever I needed, as far as additional equipment, weapons, and ammunition were concerned, could be obtained by contacting General Ratko Mladic. This was his responsibility. They had already spoken to him about this matter, and General Petar Gracanin had told him that we would be arriving in Sarajevo and that if we needed anything, we should contact him in order to receive weapons and ammunition from him in good time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, sir, if you could go to the next reference to your name, down below that, where Mr. Gracanin mentions your name again. And if you would read that one and the next two -- or the next three boxes following.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can I read it out now?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: "Okay ..." That's what Stanisic said, Mico Stanisic. Petar Gracanin replies: "Okay. We'll by in touch. Let Davidovic go to see Mladic and report to him personally." Stanisic says, "Agreed." Gracanin then says, "Let him tell him that I spoke to him." "Did you speak to Mladic?" "Yes."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all I have to ask you about that one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One question for you, Mr. Hannis, the -- the conversation is dated 00.05.1992. Is that for an unknown date in the month of May 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's understood. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I should indicate to Your Honour it that has the date the 19th of May in his authentication sheet which was done at that time based on, I think, his conversations in connection with another conversation on the 19th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Davidovic, did you go find General Mladic and have a conversation with him?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I found him and I told him who I was. I told him where I had come from. He said he had spoken to Petar Gracanin and he said that if I needed anything, I should contact him and he would help me. The relationship was very correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, in your statement at paragraph 54, you talk about going to find him. Where did you find him?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I found him in the Lukavica barracks, which is where the regular army used to be based in Sarajevo, and that's where the command of that unit had previously been located.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when you found him there and had a conversation with him, was there anybody else present during your conversation with Mr. -- with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We started a conversation and then Mr. Karadzic joined in. He entered the premises, greeted, greeted Mladic, and he joined in the conversation that General Mladic and I were having.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Was it just the three of you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Had you ever met either one of them before this occasion?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I never spoke to them personally, but I had had prior contact with them. I knew Karadzic when he -- from the time he came to Belgrade, but I never had direct contact with him. That was the first time that the three of us had direct contact, the first time I had direct contact with General Mladic and the first time I had direct contact with Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: From your statement, it appears this meeting occurred after you had complained to Gracanin about what you had seen at Vrace. Did you tell Mladic and Karadzic anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours, just before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: -- the witness continues to answer that question, there are matters that have been excised from the statement specifically because they're not appropriate to 89(F). In those circumstances, the evidence should be led viva voce and a question: Did you tell Mladic and Karadzic anything about that is not appropriate in the circumstances, Your Honour. It should be: What was the conversation? Simple, open question. Not leading, Your Honour. And I object to questions on those specific areas that are not subject to 89(F) being the subject of leading questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, where you said it appears that this meeting occurred after you had complained about something, then it's still not clear to the Chamber, of course, what were complaints about. The most appropriate would have been to ask the witness for the subject of the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, can you tell us what you said to General Mladic and Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I told General Mladic about certain things. I had started to speak to him when Mr. Karadzic entered the premises. I said that I had noticed that there was a lot of crime, looting, that flats were being broken into. There were all sorts of things taking place, and most of all looting. I said that the property had to be protected. People were breaking into flats and taking items out of these flats in Sarajevo, et cetera, and I thought that Mr. Ratko Mladic should be informed of the fact. He said that it was necessary to establish some kind of a central warehouse where this sort of property would be taken to. There was all sorts of stuff, televisions, furniture, et cetera, and this should then be distributed to wounded soldiers. And Mr. Karadzic also said that some sort of solution would be found to protect this property in some way so that it could be put to good use, so that the troops and the people could make good use of this property. This was the subject of the discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At what point in time in your conversation with General Mladic did Mr. Karadzic come into the room?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: As I said, when I started speaking to Ratko Mladic, Karadzic entered the room and he joined in the conversation. He was informed of the problem I was talking about and we continued to discuss this subject, how to prevent the looting of property. Karadzic and Mladic confirmed the fact that such things were happening and that this was quite noticeable.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did -- did you make any suggestion about what should be done about the problem?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I said that it had to be prevented. I must admit that we weren't really involved in protecting the front lines but the policemen I saw there were mostly involved in looting and breaking into flats and stealing things. And when I saw the demarcation line, I could see people taking goods -- unloading goods from some kind of a lorry. It was a very difficult situation. You could see people who were -- who were crying, who were distressed, and armed individuals were mostly involved in such acts. At least, that's what I noticed. There were members of the police force in police uniforms involved in such acts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How did -- how did your discussion end? Was there any agreement reached about what to do about the problem?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the conversation ended by Mr. Karadzic saying that there were quite a few problems there and that something had to be done, and he said that he would talk to the head of government, Djeric and that a solution had to be found which would be satisfactory in terms of the needs of both the armed forces and the people. And General Ratko Mladic said that it had to be stopped and that any stuff that was found and found to have been stolen would have to be placed into some kind of central warehouse and that it was one in a range of problems. And then they continued to talk and I left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask one question: Mr. Davidovic, what in your view as a policeman would be a proper response to looting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there's no proper response. There's only one response: To stop looting and to implement the necessary measures. That's the only thing you can do, put a stop to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What do you understand to be the -- the measures to be taken? As you said, "necessary measures."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I mean is that the police officers should arrest those people and start proceedings and take them in and keep them in custody and make it impossible for them to continue to engage in looting. This is something that can't be tolerated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was that discussed, whether or not those who were found to be looting would be arrested or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What was the content of the discussion in that respect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, actually not about them being arrested. It was mentioned that certain checkpoints should be set up in order to make it impossible to access that area where war was going on and that any such looted goods would be impounded at those checkpoints. Nobody mentioned arresting those individuals. It was only about the goods because this was a generally accepted attitude, as it were, and Mr. Karadzic mentioned it in the course of that conversation. He said, "We should not allow for any sort of conflict to arise between Serbs -- amongst Serbs." It was very important for Serbs not to fight one another, as had been the case in some other conflicts in our part of the world, such as during the Second World War. So that's what he said. But that checkpoints should be set up in order for the looted goods to be impounded, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to ask an additional question now. Who could have taken it upon themselves considering the balance of power? The existing balance of power at the time, who could have take it upon themselves to make those arrests? What service -- what force would have been able to put a stop to such activity? Looting, I mean.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was -- well, the only service would have been the police force. They had a sufficient staff and equipment and they were the only ones who were actually professionally prepared to do that. They were the only ones who could have done it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And with regard to these people engaging in such acts, did the regular police force, if I may say so, did they have sufficient power to intervene? What I mean is, for example, you referred to a unit of Red Berets of about 50 men, and you said that that unit was made up of criminals for the most part. Would the police still have had the possibility and the ability to react in the face of such an armed group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether I've made myself quite clear, but I'm trying to make it clear now. Well, all this looting was mostly perpetrated by police officers. They were wearing uniforms. And during -- I mean, these were people who became police officers overnight and there was no other unit, no other force that could have countered that because they had been incorporated within the regular police force. But considering the command structure, the police force still could have stopped this but no effort was made to put a stop to this. Quite the contrary. They actually encouraged police officers to engage in looting and stealing. And I'll tell you why: On a number of occasions, I heard superiors within the same ministry say to police officers, "We won't interfere with you taking any stuff for your own needs but you must do what we tell you to do." So this conflict, as it were -- well, basically they were being asked to take sides and to fight on the side of that particular authority and policy. And for that reason, it might well have happened that -- I mean, that's why it happened that this group behaved as it did, the group that came from Belgrade. I myself witnessed something like that. On one evening, there was this group around the place called Carli and they were bringing in some technical equipment and they had some kind of warehouse where they stored it. And I think they had found somewhere a robe belonging to a Catholic priest. And this person called Carli put it on and walked around dressed like that. And he was mocking it. And that behaviour was quite beyond the pale, if you think in terms of normal human relations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, I want to go now to paragraph 56 of your statement. Did you have later on occasion to be involved in discussions about evacuating the JNA from barracks in which they were located in Sarajevo at this time, in -- in May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, please. I haven't quite understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. In your statement at paragraph 56, you talk about being involved in discussions about evacuating the JNA from barracks in Sarajevo and you mention going to Lukavica with Milenko Karisik and meeting with Colonel Stupar. First of all, can you tell me, who was Milenko Karisik? What agency was he a part of?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: This requires a somewhat lengthy answer, because you've asked quite a few questions here. Let me tell you first: I participated in talks which were held between I, myself, and Milenko Karisik, who was a commander of a special unit within the MUP of the republic, and at a later stage, Mr. Stupar -- I think it was -- he was a lieutenant or a lieutenant colonel from the JNA. And he came to Sarajevo and to Pale and he was at the school in Vrace, where the unit was being prepared for taking the Marsal Tito Barracks in Sarajevo and for the soldiers, officers, and their families who were there to be taken out of the barracks and taken to the Republika Srpska and Serbia. And that was the first time that I met Mr. Stupar and Karisik was there throughout, since he was the commander. He had been appointed commander of that special unit because their own commander, Mr. Rapija [phoen], who was the commander up until then, well, he had been wounded in the operation that was aimed at taking the school at Vrace and so he had to be hospitalised. And Karisik was then appointed commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you mentioned this particular that was discussed. Why -- what was happening at that time? Why was it necessary to try and have a plan to evacuate the JNA from the barracks, from the Marsal Tito Barracks?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: And we're talking about the beginning of the war here. Within this barracks, Marsal Tito Barracks, the barracks were surrounded by either the Patriotic League or the newly set up Armed Forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I can't tell you with any degree of certainty. But at any rate, the barracks was in Sarajevo in the part controlled by either the Patriotic League or the armed forces and they surrounded it and they did not allow for any contact with the outside world. They made it impossible for people to go in and out. There was shooting every day and their electricity and water supplies had been cut off. Since there was a large group of soldiers within those barracks, the aim was for the barracks to be taken and for both the army personnel and the civilians to be enabled to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was that plan carried out, the plan to take the barracks?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Why not, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Of course. The plan had been devised, and I think it had been completed -- I mean, the plan. The plan was for the school at Vrace to go and cross Miljacka, the river, to go through the barracks and go to Han [phoen].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, may I stop you. The question was why the plan was not carried out. In your response you now describe what the plan was. Could you please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The plan was never carried out because General -- Major General Boskovic at the time came to Sarajevo bearing a decision from the Presidency of the former Yugoslavia, as he said, with -- with explicit orders that armed conflict should be avoided and that we should not try and take the barracks but that he would engage on talks and on the basis of the outcome of those talks those people could then be moved out and for the armed attack to be avoided. And that was the reason why the plan was never implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: After this change of plans when General Boskovic came, did you later have a conversation with Mico Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what was you -- what were you asked or tasked to do now in the Republika Srpska with your group of men that had come from the federal SUP?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: My task upon arriving at the republic SUP was to train a special police unit and to assist in organising and training of the MUP officers within the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you do that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was my main task.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how long did it take you to do that, approximately?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: As soon as we got there, we started to look at the situation and try and see how many people from the previous special units had remained within the Republika Srpska. I think it was about a dozen people there. And then we started planning for that unit to include about 100 people. The MUP gave us a list of either volunteers, people who volunteered to join this special unit. And they, of course, had to be either athletes or have some kind of sports background or some martial arts or whatever and that they would then be trained and taught how to use weapons and then they would be trained as members of the special unit. And we got more than 100 volunteers who came forward and became members of that unit. The training took place in the following way: One of them and one of us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think you've gone on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, again, may I stop you. The question to you was: When you said that your task was to train a special police unit and to assist in organising and training of the MUP officers, you were asked "How long did it take you to do that, approximately?" So how much time? And you now in full detail are explaining to us what it all included. If Mr. Hannis would like to more -- to know more details about what the training exactly was about, he'll ask you. What he did ask you at this moment was how much time that took. And may I ask you to focus very much on the question while answering it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you remember how long -- how long you spent approximately in this training process? Was it days or weeks or months?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Approximately three weeks. Three weeks tops. We would have needed much longer, but that's what we had available. And after those three weeks, we were asked to do other things, and so that's where we had a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what was the next thing that you were asked to do?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: They asked us to go to the front line and participate in this conflict and to hold the front line at -- at the Jelenska Globlje [phoen].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, at the Jewish cemetery.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And how long were you and your men at the Jewish cemetery, approximately?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Two to three days. We had already left on the third day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you talk to your boss, Petar Gracanin, about that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I gave him all the details and I asked what to do next. I said that I was not an expert on those matters, the front line and all that, and that I had originally been sent down there to do other things. And then he initially agreed. He said he would get in touch with Mico Stanisic, and then we talked to him as well and then I was moved somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: After this conversation with Gracanin, did you have a personal conversation with Mico Stanisic about what you should do next, other than hold the front line at the Jewish cemetery?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I asked Mico to give me some police tasks. But obviously at that point in time they did not need a policeman. They needed something else, because they had enough people to carry out those police duties. But originally those people were engaged doing other things. They were driving golf carts to Belgrade [as interpreted] and they wanted to send us to hold the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What was your next task in the general vicinity?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: There was no other task, and we were asked to go to Jahorina, where there was the seat of the government and the Presidency, and we were asked to provide security there for the Presidency. And we went to Jahorina, and I think we staid at a hotel called Bistrica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you mentioned that the government and the Presidency were located there at that time? What was -- can you describe for the Court what the atmosphere was like or what the situation was.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I can briefly. That hotel and another hotel - I can't remember what it's called; it was at a slightly higher altitude - that's where the seat of government was situated, and there were always quite a few people there, women, and there was a restaurant there. And people used to eat and drink a great deal. And there were lots of people. And there was a state of chaos, which in my view properly depicted the overall situation characterising Bosnia and Herzegovina, not just the Republika Srpska. There was a lot of confusion and people were sitting around talking and -- even the president of -- the head of government at that time, Mr. Djeric, that I spoke to -- I mean, I said, "Well, what's going on here? Everything's falling to piece and there are all these comings and goings and we don't know what's going on." And he said, "Yes, it is quite clear to me, yeah, that something will have to be done."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you -- did you report this situation to Mr. Gracanin?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In your statement, you say that you kept copies of these reports but you don't have them any longer. Why is that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I did write a report and sent it to the minister. It was dispatched to the minister. And I asked for instructions on what to do next. And I gave a detailed account of what was going on and what my view was. That document went to the federal minister and I had a copy, but that copy afterwards was taken away from me and I never managed to find it again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, it's -- it's close to 12.30. If we would have a break for 20 minutes, we would have one hour remaining. Looking, for example, at your last question, Mr. Hannis, there's a clear answer to that question in the statement, which is part of the 89(F), so looking at the clock, looking at where you approximately are, I wonder whether such questions are necessary not because the information is not perhaps assisting the Prosecution's case but since it's clearly in the -- in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You're right, Your Honour. I was looking at the paragraph above, which was part of the redaction. And I -- I missed that this is not in the redacted portion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. This is --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is in the statement and it's not something I need to ask him about here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please keep that in mind because from what I understood was your time assessment, if I look at the clock and where we are in the statement, Ms. Loukas might not be too unhappy that you would need some extra time, but the Chamber would like to have the evidence to be presented as efficiently as possible. We'll adjourn until quarter to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, before we broke, you were talking about your time at Mount Jahorina and activities you observed there. What kind of activities was it that you felt it was necessary to file reports about? You described it was chaotic and that there were women there, but that doesn't seem to be unusual for a wartime situation.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether I've been clear. "Chaotic" means it was in total disarray. I could see the Prime Minister there, representatives from the government, people sitting in the cafe. Some unknown people were arriving there. Certain things were going on. And as far as I could see, it didn't seem as if everything was functioning properly. I was referring to women, wives, who were present in a chaotic situation and life was not really going on as usual in the cafes and restaurants.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you say certain things were going on, are they things that you believed to be criminal activity?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to the phraseology of that question now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas -- Witness Davidovic, you said that "life was not really going on as usual in the cafes and restaurants," which is a rather vague expression. What exactly did you observe that needed reporting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I said that I noticed that the state bodies and the state as such were not functioning. Why did I say that? Because the bodies, the organs that were supposed to be functioning properly from the police and the state bodies, including the government bodies, et cetera, well, they weren't functioning in the way they should have been functioning. Each department should have functioned in its own manner. The police was in a state of total chaos. Citizens would appear, ask for certain certificates, for authorisation, et cetera, et cetera. And as a result no one knew where people were residing. It was quite difficult to define the situation. Everything was taking place in the street, in restaurants, in cafes. Armed groups of people, armed individuals, would appear. Certain formations would appear. No one knew who they were or why they had come.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. When you said that the police was not functioning and was in a total -- a state of total chaos, what kind of police functions were not performed or fulfilled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, for example, buildings were not protected. Institutions were not protected. Individuals who were there were not protected by the police. None of these duties were performed. One knows how one is to enter buildings, how individuals are to be received, and one knows what sort of duties the police should usually perform, regardless of whether the police force was established before the war or during wartime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Hannis -- Judge Hanoteau has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You said that copies of this report disappeared when your flat was searched in Belgrade in 1995, and you said that this search had been organised by the MUP, by the Serbian MUP. I have a number of questions with regard to this subject. How did you know that the search had been organised by the Serbian MUP? What went missing from your house? And is it only the reports that were taken, that disappeared? If you could please answer that question, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When they entered the flat, they introduced themselves as MUP officials. They showed their identity cards and the search warrant that they had. They didn't provide this to -- to me. But when they entered the flat, they tried to find out where my documents were, and that's what the search was interested in. After they had finished the search, they issued a certificate which showed that they had taken items that were of interest to the Davidovic case in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So there were other documents apart from the copies of the report that were taken away by these individuals who carried out the search.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as other documents are concerned, they took my two official pistols and they took the documents from Bosnia. Nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, in paragraph 62 of your statement, you talked about when you left after this exercise, and upon returning you say you were instructed to leave behind your weapons and equipment, including the five pinzgauers. Who instructed you to leave that equipment behind with the RS MUP?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: The federal secretary, Petar Gracanin, instructed me to do this. He did this personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I want to move on to after your return -- well, before you had left, you say in your statement that you had made a trip to Bijeljina before this first visit to the Republika Srpska after the war started. And in paragraph 65, you talk about being at the SUP building in Bijeljina with Cedo Kljajic. You describe him selecting out vehicles and writing down chassis numbers. Do you recall that incident? These were the seized vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Kljajic and I left Sarajevo, Pale. We went down there with the unit. And I drove to Bijeljina. The reason was to see what accommodation was available since in Bijeljina a few years prior to the war a new SUP building had been built which was quite functional. It had been built for the organs of the internal affairs and the Republika Srpska Ministry of the Interior was to move -- or be transferred to Bijeljina. That's why I went there. And when I arrived there, I then saw that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I have to stop you again. The question was specifically about selection of vehicles and writing down chassis numbers, and the question was whether these were seized vehicles. In your answer, you deal with a lot of other matters. Could I ask you: Were these seized vehicles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, these vehicles had been seized from individuals who had committed offences of some kind and they were on the grounds of the SUP and they took down the chassis number, the number of the engine, so that such numbers would be included in the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In that paragraph 65, you indicate that Mr. Kljajic was falsifying vehicle registrations on blank registration forms. Did you ask him about why he was doing that? And if so, what did he say?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I entered the office and I saw Kljajic there. He was typing out details into new driving licence form. I asked him what he was doing and I asked him why he was typing out driving licences, because he was a high-ranking official. And he said that Mico Stanisic had authorised him to do that. They had to live in a normal way. They had to have something to live off. And this is probably why he was typing this out, in order to sell these items and obtain resources in this way. And this was subsequently confirmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In paragraph 64 through 66, you talk about visiting the SUP in Bijeljina and finding that Arkan's men had taken over. Did you -- did you report this fact to anyone?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And there's a detailed report about that. When I arrived there, I saw a group of individuals, some of whom I knew from before. There was a colonel there in Arkan's army. He later became a general. I saw Sasa there, a special police commander in that body, and there were some other individuals among whom I recognised Legija.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We do have the details about that in your statement, and that is in evidence and the Judges can -- can read that, so I will try and focus my questions on things that are not in the portion of the redacted statement we gave them. Who did you report to about that fact, that the -- Arkan's men had taken over the SUP in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I informed my minister and I informed Mico Stanisic, as the Minister of the Internal Affairs of Republika Srpska, and he was aware of the fact. He knew that they were there and that they were in power. Cedo Kljajic was the assistant, was someone I couldn't convince of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you get any response to your report about the presence of Arkan's men in the Bijeljina SUP from either Mico Stanisic or from your boss, Mr. Gracanin?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't. Mico Stanisic commented. That's all. He said, "I know there's nothing else we can do. That's how it has to be."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, in the interest of time, I've decided to skip a couple items that were on my list. And for the purposes of the court reporter and the registry, I want to go to item number 13 on the list I had previously provided them. It's a newspaper article from a publication called, I think, Muslimanski Glas. This is dated the 12th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, I think you've had a chance to look at this before.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This article describes the presence and the individuals associated with a number of paramilitary groups, many of whom are reportedly from the Republic of Serbia. Did you have a chance to read this article before today?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No. I saw this a few days ago. Or to be more precise, the day before yesterday. That's when I read through it. But this is probably a newspaper of some kind from the Federation, an article which refers to the groups present in the territory of Republika Srpska. He mentions Arkan's men, Seselj's men, the White Eagles, volunteers, et cetera, royalists, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I can stop you there.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: And it's numbered 1 to 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there and ask you a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But before I do, could I ask for the number that would be assigned to this one.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. It will be Exhibit P770.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In terms of what the article says about the groups that were present and the individuals who were the heads of those groups, based on your knowledge, is it accurate in that regard? Just in terms of the names of the groups and the people that were leading those groups.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's accurate.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, just in relation to that, I think firstly there's quite a broad category here there's quite a list. And in -- in terms of the fact that we are dealing with a newspaper article. We are dealing with an article that was produced during the war. And as we all know, the first casualty of war is truth. So I think Mr. Hannis should be a little bit more defined in terms of which particular aspects he's talking about here, because there's quite a list there - one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine - it's not clear from the question and thereby not the answer what actual groups and leaders are being referred to here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From what I understood, it's the whole list.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, if -- that's where the confusion comes in, Your Honour, because there's -- the whole list does not include leaders in some categories. So therefore --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But of course --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: -- it is confusing and amorphous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But of course -- of course the witness could not be expected to confirm the correctness of a leader which is not mentioned. It's about groups. It's about leaders. And to the extent that leaders are mentioned, I take it that the witness confirms that these were leaders of those groups. And where there are no leaders mentioned, there -- of course there's nothing to confirm. Is -- Mr. Davidovic, when you said "it's accurate," did you mean to say that the names of the groups were accurate or the -- I would say, the description sometimes where not a name is given is accurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, they are accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To the extent that leaders were mentioned, are these leaders mentioned correctly in relation to the groups they are linked to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. And that is the order they appear on, the order they appear on is based on the strength of these groups.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that's true for all the nine groups mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: There's just one further matter, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: It's -- "We will require further information from the Prosecution as to the -- where this newspaper article appears." In the list of exhibit, it's got Glas or Glasnik. It's -- it hasn't been refined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis said that it was Muslimanski Glas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Muslimanski Glas, that's what he said. But it's -- is it Glas or Glasnik? That's what it says in the exhibit list. It leaves it open, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The document information sheet I have for this item, Your Honour, indicates that this is an article from 12 June 1992 from Muslimanski Glas or Glasnik, and I don't know if that's because the copy we have was somewhat illegible and the title couldn't be read, but that's what I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you could find the front page of that newspaper or periodical.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will do some further research with our open sources --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- section, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And also, just in relation to this, Your Honour, a marker: Seeking to confirm matters contained in a newspaper article in a sort of global way, without confirming from the witness what his precise knowledge and is how he could actually confirm the contents of a newspaper in this way, is, in my submission, a rather too-broad way of trying to confirm the sort of matters that are contained in a newspaper article and would not be of great assistance to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, of course, the knowledge of the witness on what happened on the ground in Bosnia and Herzegovina is in some detail set out in his statement. At the same time, Ms. Loukas, I tend to agree with you that getting spontaneous answers from the witness, instead of let him confirm lists in newspapers, might have a greater value to the Chamber. At the same time, Ms. Loukas, the whole issue of spontaneous coming up with answers is, of course, in a system where the parties spend hours and days on proofing sessions is a bit limited, if you look at the origin of the value of such trial techniques.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, at the same time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me say the following: I have worked -- no. I have observed how a pathologist in the Belgian criminal proceedings would give the details of the post-mortem. These were pathologists who were not allowed to consult any papers because you had to elicit that information from such an expert witness without him consulting any papers. I once spoke to the daughter of such a pathologist, who told me that her father would be learning by heart, exact, the numbers of how many blood there was in the left chamber of the heart, how many -- so that he could reproduce that the next morning without any mistake. Of course, I just would like to put the trial technique in which you elicit from the witness the answer that comes up on the basis of the non-leading question in some perspective. Having done so, you may proceed, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, can I just make one quick comment in relation to that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I'll allow you to make a comment in relation to that after you have thought it over for 24 hours. So I'm not -- it's not a debating club here, as you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I am open for any comment but rather not enter into a debate at this moment. Please proceed, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. And I'm happy to take on board what Your Honour has indicated. But -- and I will be providing further comment with the opportunity of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: -- the 24 hours. But nevertheless one important rule is the evidence must come from the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Not from the mouth of the Prosecutor, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But here it comes from the newspaper article and then confirmation by the witness. The newspaper article will be an exhibit, and the witness -- but I said already that it's of greater value to receive that evidence in a different way.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So to that extent, you got some support.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, in that article, later on in the English - it's page 2, the last full paragraph at the bottom of the page - it mentions Petar Gracanin having sent to Bosnia-Herzegovina a special unit of 150 men. Your unit was a special unit, but how many men did you have in your unit?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: There were members of the special force units in my unit, and there were 14 or 15 men in this unit at the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So this article, in terms of your unit's presence in Bosnia, exaggerates the numbers by a factor of 10; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. It says 150 men, and that is totally absurd.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And with regard to the number of Arkan's and Seselj's that were mentioned in the article, did you find that the numbers were exaggerated by a similar factor?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. And that's what I said. There were -- it says that there were several thousand men. It says that Arkan had 2.000 men, and then it says that he had 8.000 Chetniks who were at the ready. I think this has been so exaggerated that it's just pointless to comment on it. Where would you find accommodation for 2.000 or 8.000 men? This is an enormous number of men and you would have to provide them with accommodation and food. So it simply doesn't make sense. Everything has been multiplied by a factor of 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me now take you back to your statement. In paragraph 70, you say that "There was also widespread looting in Bijeljina as you had -- as there had been in Pale." Do you know -- well, how do you know about this looting in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I have to say that I lived in Bijeljina, as did my family, and every weekend, when it was possible for me to go to Bijeljina, I went there. And when I performed my official tasks -- well, I could observe this when I went there over the weekend, and I realised that this was taking place when I spoke to various people. People would approach me. There were lots of questions that they would ask me. They would ask what to do. So I could observe this directly and I also heard about it when I spoke to various people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You say in that paragraph that this looting was organised, and you describe one Vojkan Djurkovic as a local man involved in the process. Do you know where that money was going that was taken as a result of this looting?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I do. It was divided into several parts. He kept one part for himself. Another part was given to Arkan. Another part was sent to Pale, to the people who had authorised him to do what he was doing. And as for the property that was there, well, there was -- there were technical goods there, et cetera. But this was mostly sold to refugees who arrived in the Bijeljina area. They arrived from Brcko, Zvornik, areas that had been caught up in the war. They would then appear and they would sell houses and property to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You said in your answer that part of it was going to "the people who had authorised him to do what he was doing." Who are those people?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, people in charge of the SDS, Krajisnik, Karadzic, people in power, Mandic, all those who took decisions. Because this wasn't only happening in Bijeljina; it was also happening in Trebinje and Zvornik, and these are the policies pursued by that party.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You talked about Bijeljina. In terms of where it's located geographically, do you know whether Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Karadzic were ever in Bijeljina during the war?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know that. I saw them myself. I had the opportunity to hear about them having been there, and on a number of occasions I saw them coming and going. Because if you travelled by car from Republika Srpska to Belgrade, you either travelled through Zvornik or Bijeljina, but normally through Bijeljina because there were no war activities there, so it was safer. So if we think in terms of war, this was a peaceful area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, you asked the witness to specify the people who had authorised him to do what he was doing. Could you also explore the source of knowledge in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, we were talking about Vojkan Djurkovic participating in this organised looting you described in Bijeljina and I asked you to tell who the persons were in Pale that you say had authorised him to do this. How do you know about that? What's your source of information for that fact?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I spoke about that in broader terms in one part of my statement. I can't remember exactly where. But if you want to talk about the goal in particular, the goal of the Serb Democratic Party in particular, it was to ethnically cleanse the area of people who were not Serbs. And for that reason it was a legitimate policy from them.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the witness is quite clearly not answering the question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: -- that was asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me reformulate the question. You said about --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will reply to the question, if I may. I would really like you to give me the opportunity to answer. You don't have to rephrase the question. I'm going to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I will rephrase the question for the following reason: Because it's a question which is complex and is -- the following: When you were referring to those people who authorised, there are two elements. The first one is that these people authorised, if I correctly understood, the looting to take place. First of all, how do you know that they authorised the looting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I myself saw a document that Vojkan Djurkovic showed to me authorising them to carry out merciful moves of people and that the police force and the armed forces should not interfere with his task, and so it was an approval which came from the cabinet and signed by Mr. Krajisnik in person, and he used to show it around and he carried it around. I was not the only person who saw that piece of paper. Other people saw it, too. And when I got in touch with Micic, who was a member of parliament, as a member of the Serb Democratic Party., he said he saw that document and he asked Mr. Krajisnik about that document and he apparently answered he did not want to interfere with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, the second issue is that you said that they profited from the looting, since part of it was made available -- part of the -- of the financial results were made available to them. How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because Vojkan Djurkovic used to say publicly that he was taking that money to Pale to Karadzic and Krajisnik, and he did it in person and also through Luka Karadzic and Momo's brother and so on. It was common knowledge. He never tried to hide it. He said it out loud.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the basis of that knowledge is what Vojkan Djurkovic told you, and you said, "He used to say publicly that he was taking the money to Pale to Karadzic and Krajisnik." And then you said, "And he did it in person." Is that what he told you, or is that what you observed yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He told me himself, and I heard it on a number of occasions when other people were talking about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: These other people, could you mention their names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course. People from Bijeljina, the people they were in touch with. I can give you the names, if you want me to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For example, a man who is in Bijeljina, Dusko Marjanovic, he's a lawyer there today. Then Gavrilovic, someone who was in charge of a unit during the war. Then people from MUP who were also involved and who witnessed that. And there were some officers there as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it from your answer that where you mentioned Marjanovic, Gavrilovic, that they told you about it but that specifically the MUP people told you that they were involved and that they were witnesses of such things to happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] MUP was directly involved in all that. There were people within MUP who did not want to get involved but they could do nothing to put a stop to it because if they tried to do something, they would be turned back and they would be subject to disciplinary measures and some of them were even sacked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
